name: Delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction
aliases: Delayed serologic and haemolytic transfusion reaction

clinicalPearls: Occurs typically several days to two weeks after transfusion due to an anamnestic antibody response against a red-cell antigen to which the recipient was previously sensitised.
Most commonly implicates antibodies of the Kidd, Rh, Duffy, Kell and MNS systems, with Kidd (anti-Jk) antibodies notorious for evanescence and for causing severe delayed reactions.
Antibody levels fall below detection between exposures, so the pre-transfusion antibody screen may be negative; the antibody reappears rapidly on re-exposure.
Presents insidiously with an unexplained fall in haemoglobin, low-grade fever, mild jaundice and a failure of transfused red cells to sustain the expected increment.
Haemolysis is predominantly extravascular, mediated by IgG-coated cells removed by the reticuloendothelial system, so overt haemoglobinuria and shock are uncommon.
A positive direct antiglobulin test with newly detectable alloantibody and spherocytes on the film supports the diagnosis.
Management is usually supportive; future transfusions must use antigen-negative units, and the antibody should be recorded permanently to prevent recurrence.
In sickle cell disease a delayed reaction can trigger hyperhaemolysis, an important and dangerous overlap to recognise.
reference.pathophysiology: A delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction reflects a secondary (anamnestic) immune response. Prior transfusion or pregnancy sensitises the recipient to a foreign red-cell antigen, but the resulting alloantibody wanes over time and may be undetectable at the next crossmatch. When antigen-positive cells are transfused, memory B cells rapidly produce IgG antibody over several days. These antibodies coat the transfused cells, which are then cleared extravascularly by splenic and hepatic macrophages via Fc-receptor-mediated phagocytosis. Because destruction is gradual and largely extravascular, the clinical picture is of a progressive unexplained anaemia with rising unconjugated bilirubin and lactate dehydrogenase rather than acute intravascular haemolysis, although brisk complement-fixing antibodies such as those of the Kidd system can occasionally produce more acute haemolysis.
additionalDifferentials: Ongoing bleeding causing a falling haemoglobin
Hyperhaemolysis syndrome in sickle cell disease
additionalInvestigations: Direct antiglobulin test on a current sample
Repeat antibody screen and identification panel comparing pre- and post-transfusion sera
Elution studies to identify antibody bound to transfused cells
Lactate dehydrogenase, bilirubin, haptoglobin and reticulocyte count
Full blood count and film for spherocytes and evidence of haemolysis
Comparison of haemoglobin increment with the expected post-transfusion value
redFlags: Unexpected drop in haemoglobin days after transfusion with jaundice
New positive direct antiglobulin test with a previously negative screen
Haemoglobinuria suggesting a more brisk haemolytic process
Rapidly worsening anaemia in a patient with sickle cell disease raising concern for hyperhaemolysis
reference.prognosis: Most delayed reactions are mild and self-limiting, resolving as the incompatible cells are cleared, provided antigen-negative blood is given thereafter. Occasionally, brisk haemolysis causes clinically significant anaemia or renal impairment, and in sickle cell disease evolution to hyperhaemolysis can be life-threatening.
pitfalls: Overlooking the diagnosis and attributing the falling haemoglobin to bleeding.
Relying on a negative pre-transfusion screen despite historical alloimmunisation.
Failing to permanently record identified antibodies, risking recurrence at other sites.
Not recognising the overlap with hyperhaemolysis in sickle cell disease.
Transfusing further antigen-positive units and compounding the haemolysis.
references: British Society for Haematology guidelines on the investigation and management of acute transfusion reactions
